title_en: Wizards of the Coast Sues Website That Prints Fake Magic: The Gathering Cards, Alleging Counterfeiting Operation
summary_en: For as much as Magic: The Gathering has grown in popularity over the last several years, the market for proxies and counterfeits has also grown. And now, Wizards of the Coast is suing PrintMTG, alleging a counterfeiting ring for the trading card game.
body_en:
For as much as Magic: The Gathering has grown in popularity over the last several years, the market for proxies and counterfeits has also grown. And now, Wizards of the Coast is suing PrintMTG, alleging a counterfeiting ring for the trading card game.
Wizards of the Coast filed the lawsuit (via Aftermath ) in its home state of Washington, alleging PrintMTG "operate as a complex and sophisticated network (...) engaged in trademark infringement, counterfeiting and criminal copyright infringement on a grand scale." Wizards seeks $28.65 million in damages.
For the most part, PrintMTG was a destination for people to print proxies, or essentially fake Magic cards that could stand in for real ones, for either playtesting or trying before you buy the actual card. And, thanks to the Reserved list, there are plenty of cards that cost thousands of dollars for a legitimate copy, so it's easy to see why going to a website and spending $0.75 on a proxy version instead was a popular choice.
In its complaint, Wizards of the Coast seems to acknowledge the purpose that proxies serve, saying "an honest proxy is a stand-in for a real card that makes no claim to authenticity by appearance or otherwise. Though proxies are prohibited in all sanctioned Magic events, Wizards recognizes that private and noncommercial proxying is a vehicle players can use to further engage with the game, not to undermine it." But, it seems PrintMTG proxies were a bit too realistic.
Later on in the complaint, Wizards of the Coast describes what it sees as a legitimate proxy, which "include writing the name of a card in marker on a basic land card or on a blank card printed for this purpose, using one genuine card to represent another or sliding a slip of notebook paper into a card sleeve." PrintMTG and other proxy-printing websites like it, will instead print Magic's art on card stock, for a price.
Wizards of the Coast alleges that PrintMTG's proxies "directly harm Wizards by displacing sales of genuine cards" and damages "retail partners who sell those cards." But even beyond that, the company alleges that these counterfeits were "creating instability and uncertainty in the very secondary markets third-party retailers rely on as a revenue center."
There's a whole Reddit community that's sprung up, /r/RealOrNotTCG , where people post pictures of Magic cards to try and figure out if they're, well, real or not. However, PrintMTG is just one of many services that print realistic Magic proxies. This is a market that's been around for years, and it seems like Wizards of the Coast is finally cracking down on it.
This lawsuit comes after Wizards of the Coast recently changed the way booster packs work, and ahead of Darkhold Destiny, its third Marvel set.
Jackie Thomas is the Senior Tech Editor at IGN and the PC components queen. She's been covering gaming hardware for more than a decade for IGN, TechRadar, Gizmodo, PC Gamer and more. You can follow her  @Jackiecobra
